title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: The flood of nations begins to subside into its normal channels. The waves of the great movement settle, and on the calm surface eddies form in which the diplomats float, imagining that it was they who caused the flood to recede.

But the smooth sea suddenly becomes turbulent again. The diplomats think their disagreements are causing this new surge; they expect war between their sovereigns; the situation seems unsolvable. But the wave they feel rising is not coming from where they expect. It rises again from the same source—from Paris. The last backwash of the movement from the west occurs: a backwash that will resolve the apparently insoluble diplomatic difficulties and put an end to the military movement of that era.

The man who had devastated France returns to France alone, without any conspiracy and without soldiers. Any guard could arrest him, but by some strange chance no one does, and everyone rapturously greets the man they had cursed the day before and would curse again within a month.
This man is still needed to justify the final collective act.
That act is performed.
The last role is played. The actor is told to take off his costume and wash off his makeup: he won't be needed anymore.

And some years pass during which this man plays a pitiful comedy alone on his island, scheming and lying to justify his actions when justification is no longer needed, and showing the whole world what it was that people had mistaken for strength when an unseen hand was guiding him.
The stage manager, having brought the drama to its close and stripped the actor, shows him to us.
"See what you believed in! This is he! Do you see now that it was not he but I who moved you?"
But dazed by the force of the movement, it was a long time before people understood this.
Still greater coherence and inevitability can be seen in the life of Alexander I, the man who stood at the head of the counter-movement from east to west.
What qualities were needed in the man who was to stand at the head of that movement from east to west, overshadowing all others?

What was needed was a sense of justice and sympathy with European affairs—but a broad sympathy, not dulled by petty interests; a moral superiority over the other sovereigns of the day; a mild and attractive personality; and a personal grievance against Napoleon. And all of this was present in Alexander I; all of it had been prepared by countless so-called coincidences throughout his earlier life: his upbringing, his liberal beginnings, the advisors who surrounded him, Austerlitz, Tilsit, and Erfurt.

During the national war he was inactive because he was not needed. But as soon as the necessity for a general European war arose, he appeared in his place at the right moment and—uniting the nations of Europe—led them to the goal.
The goal is reached. After the final war of 1815, Alexander possesses all possible power. How does he use it?

Alexander I—the peacemaker of Europe, the man who from his youth had striven only for his people's welfare, the originator of liberal reforms in his own country—now that he seemed to possess the power and therefore the ability to bring about the welfare of his people, while Napoleon in exile was making plans that would infallibly have made nations happy had he been able to carry them out—Alexander, having fulfilled his mission and feeling the hand of God upon him, suddenly recognizes the insignificance of that apparent power, turns away from it, hands it over to despicable men, and says only:
"Not unto us, not unto us, but unto Thy name!... I too am just a man like the rest of you. Let me live like a man and think of my soul and of God."

Just as the sun and each atom of light is a sphere complete in itself, yet at the same time only a part of a whole too vast for man to comprehend, so each individual carries within himself his own aims while serving a larger purpose that lies beyond human understanding.

A bee landing on a flower stings a child. And the child is afraid of bees and declares that bees exist to sting people. A poet admires the bee drinking nectar from the flower and says bees exist to gather the fragrance of flowers. A beekeeper, noticing that the bee collects pollen and brings it to the hive, says that the bee's purpose is to gather honey. Another beekeeper, who has studied the life of the swarm more closely, says the bee gathers pollen to feed the young and rear a queen—that its purpose is the continuation of the species. A botanist notices that the pollen-dusted bee fertilizes the pistil of a flower, and he sees this as the bee's purpose. Another, observing the migration of plants, sees that the bee helps in this process, and he may say that this is the bee's purpose. But the ultimate purpose of the bee is not limited to any single one of these things that human reason can discover. The higher the human intellect rises in the discovery of such purposes, the more obvious it becomes that the ultimate purpose is beyond our reach.
All that is accessible to us is the relationship between the life of the bee and other forms of life. And so it is with the purpose of historical figures and nations.
